## Limits

### Defined near a point

We say $f$ is *defined near $a$* if it is defined on some open interval containing $a$, except possibly at $a$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/02-limits.qmd)

### Limit (informal)

We write $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ if the values of $f(x)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $L$ by taking *all* $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, with $x\ne a$. We also write $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to a$. If no such real number $L$ exists, the finite limit does not exist (DNE).

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/02-limits.qmd) · [Examples](../lectures/02-limits.qmd#limits-and-function-values)

### One-sided limits

The *left-hand limit* $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L$ means $f(x)\to L$ as $x$ approaches $a$ through values $x<a$. The *right-hand limit* $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L$ uses values $x>a$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/02-limits.qmd#one-sided-limits)

### Infinite limits

We write $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty$ if outputs exceed every positive bound for all sufficiently nearby $x\ne a$.

We write $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=-\infty$ if outputs fall below every negative bound for all sufficiently nearby $x\ne a$.

Similarly for $x\to a^-$ and $x\to a^+$. Infinity describes unbounded behavior; it is not a real-number limit.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/03-infinite-limits.qmd#infinite-limits-and-vertical-asymptotes)

### Vertical asymptote

The line $x=a$ is a *vertical asymptote* if at least one of the one-sided limits at $a$ is $\infty$ or $-\infty$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/03-infinite-limits.qmd#infinite-limits-and-vertical-asymptotes)

### Indeterminate form

An expression such as $0/0$ obtained by substitution does not determine the limit. Further analysis is needed.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/04-limit-laws.qmd#indeterminate-forms-and-simplifying)

## Continuity

### Continuity at a point

A function $f$ is *continuous at $a$* if

$$
\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).
$$

This requires $f(a)$ to be defined, the limit to exist as a finite number, and the two to agree.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#continuity-at-a-point)

### One-sided continuity

A function is *right-continuous at $a$* if $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)$, and *left-continuous at $a$* if $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#one-sided-continuity)

### Continuity on an interval

A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every interior point (a point that is not an endpoint), with right-continuity at an included left endpoint and left-continuity at an included right endpoint.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#one-sided-continuity)

### Removable discontinuity

A *removable discontinuity* at $a$ occurs when the finite limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from that limit.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#types-of-discontinuities)

### Jump discontinuity

A *jump discontinuity* at $a$ occurs when the two one-sided limits are finite and unequal.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#types-of-discontinuities)

### Infinite discontinuity

An *infinite discontinuity* at $a$ occurs when at least one one-sided limit is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#types-of-discontinuities)

## Derivatives

### Secant line, average rate of change, and difference quotient

A *secant line* passes through two distinct points on a graph. Its slope is the *average rate of change*. For inputs $a$ and $a+h$, the *difference quotient* is

$$
\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},\qquad h\ne0.
$$

Slope has units of output units per input unit.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/02-limits.qmd)

### Derivative at a point and differentiability

The *derivative of $f$ at $a$*, read “$f$ prime at $a$,” is

$$
f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}
=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

provided the limit exists as a finite number. The two forms agree by setting $h=x-a$.
We say $f$ is *differentiable at $a$* when $f'(a)$ exists.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/09-derivative-at-a-point.qmd#the-derivative-at-a-point) · [Examples](../lectures/09-derivative-at-a-point.qmd#computing-derivatives-from-the-definition)

### Tangent line and instantaneous rate of change

When $f'(a)$ exists, it is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $(a,f(a))$, and the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ there. The tangent line has equation

$$
y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a).
$$

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/11-differentiation-rules.qmd#tangent-lines-and-prescribed-slopes)

### Derivative function

For a function $f$, the *derivative function* $f'$ is defined by

$$
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.
$$

Its domain consists of the points $x$ where this limit exists as a finite number.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/10-derivative-function.qmd#section-3.2-the-derivative-function)

### Higher-order derivatives

The *second derivative* $f''$ is the derivative of $f'$. The *third derivative* $f'''$ is the derivative of $f''$. Repeating this process gives the $n$th derivative, written $f^{(n)}$.

For $y=f(x)$, the notation $y'$, $f'(x)$, and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ denotes the first derivative; $y''$, $f''(x)$, and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ denotes the second derivative.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/10-derivative-function.qmd#higher-order-derivatives) · [Notation](../lectures/10-derivative-function.qmd#notation)

## Motion and special functions

### Velocity, speed, and acceleration

For a position function $s(t)$,

$$
v(t)=s'(t),\qquad \text{speed}=|v(t)|,\qquad a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t),
$$

where the derivatives exist. The sign of velocity gives direction. If position is measured in meters and time in seconds, velocity has units m/s, speed has units m/s, and acceleration has units m/s$^2$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/12-rates-of-change.qmd#from-derivatives-to-motion)

### Trigonometric functions and radians

Angles are measured in **radians**; one full turn is $2\pi$ radians. On the unit circle, the point at angle $x$ has coordinates $(\cos x,\sin x)$.

$$
\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x},\qquad \sec x=\frac1{\cos x}\qquad(\cos x\ne0),
$$

$$
\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x},\qquad \csc x=\frac1{\sin x}\qquad(\sin x\ne0).
$$

The symbols $\sec$ and $\csc$ denote reciprocals, not inverse functions. A square such as $\sin^2x$ means $(\sin x)^2$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/13-trigonometric-derivatives.qmd#trigonometric-notation-we-will-use)

### Inverse function

An inverse function *undoes* the original function:

$$
f^{-1}(f(x))=x,\qquad f(f^{-1}(y))=y.
$$

 Here $f$ must be one-to-one on the domain being used. The notation $f^{-1}$ means the inverse function, not the reciprocal $1/f$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/15-inverse-functions.qmd#inverse-functions)

### Exponential and logarithmic functions

For $a>0$, the exponential function is $f(x)=a^x$. Its domain is $\mathbb R$. When $a\ne1$, its range is $(0,\infty)$ and its inverse is $\log_a x$:

$$
y=\log_a x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a^y=x,\qquad x>0.
$$

The logarithm has domain $(0,\infty)$ and range $\mathbb R$. The base $a=1$ gives the constant exponential function $f(x)=1$, which has no inverse on $\mathbb R$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#review)

### Euler’s number

The unique positive real number $e$ for which 

$$
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=1
$$

 is called *Euler's number*.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#what-is-e) · [Supporting lemmas](theorems.qmd#exponential-slope-and-the-existence-of-e)

### Natural logarithm

The *natural logarithm* is $\ln x=\log_e x$, the inverse of $e^x$. Thus

$$
e^{\ln x}=x\quad(x>0),\qquad \ln(e^x)=x\quad(x\in\mathbb R).
$$

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#review)

### Relative growth rate

For a positive quantity $P(t)$, its relative growth rate is $P'(t)/P(t)$. If $P(t)=P_0e^{kt}$ with $P_0>0$ and $k$ constant, then

$$
\frac{P'(t)}{P(t)}=k.
$$

Here $k>0$ gives growth and $k<0$ gives decay.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#relative-growth)

## Precalculus

### Function, domain, and range

A *function* assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. The *domain* is the set of allowed inputs; the *range* is the set of outputs the function actually produces. The notation $f(x)$ means the output corresponding to input $x$. A point on its graph has coordinates $(x,f(x))$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/00-functions.qmd#functions-domain-and-range)

### Composition

The *composition* $(g\circ h)(x)=g(h(x))$ applies $h$ first and then applies $g$ to the result. Read from the inside out. The order generally matters.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/00-functions.qmd#composition-of-functions)

### One-to-one function

A function is *one-to-one* if different inputs always have different outputs.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/00-functions.qmd#one-to-one-functions-and-domain-restrictions)

:::
